en: Vīratantra

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Guru. I bow to Śiva—the cause of all, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, known as the Great Liṅga—who is worshipped by those seeking liberation; and to the Guru, who is beginningless, stainless, moving, and solely intent upon supreme grace.
I bow down to Maheśvara, the renowned Siddha who destroys [suffering] in the world and is honored by those who offer salutations. || 2 ||

I bow to him who has received instruction from the waves of the spontaneous, compassionate side-glances of Śrī Toṭaka Siddha— the sovereign of the Self, whose playful form is the primordial moving and unmoving universe.
The teachings that are well-blowing winds for one's own devotees, which are appropriate for the illustrious Vīraśaiva.
May that Murigā Śrī Śāntavīrayati bestow upon me stainless awakening. || 3 ||
Śāntavīra has become a vessel for the abundant and supreme compassion of his guru on all sides.
I bow to that Guru, Siddha, and Preceptor who has attained detachment upon this earth.
One who has attained the glory of Śiva through the grace of a Guru perfected in yoga and perfected in spiritual instruction.
The city of nectar, which delights in awakening one to reality, prospers for Vīracenna Basava. || 5 ||
The virtuous Paṇḍita, named Muragaya, questioned such a teacher with longing.
"Tell me that supreme truth, which is of such a nature and is praised by the virtuous. || 6 ||
Thus, having uttered those questions concerning the conduct of the one named Muriga, the Guru gave the corresponding answers in succession.
"Expounding a work that follows the Vedas and Āgamas, I shall speak; listen," he said with joy.

[This work] is filled with hundreds of unsurpassed and supreme methods for the practice of Rūpākṣa—the singular Great Liṅga—which is distinguished by the eight syllables and the fivefold conduct well-known throughout all the Śrutis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas.

The hand of Śakti, which serves as the means for presenting the categories of reality (*padārtha*)— consisting of the distinctions between knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*)— as taught in the Siddhānta scriptures that establish the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*).

The venerable Vīraśaiva, who is endowed with the knowledge of qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita) through the mental state of having as his sole place of worship and adoration the *bhāvaliṅga*— which consists of the *prāṇaliṅga* and the *bhūteṣṭaliṅga*, which are composed of parts and locations divided into six types based on the reliance on the investigation of the meaning of the words of the oral mantra— is the most excellent of all.
For it is said thus in the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā:
Endowed with the eightfold enclosure and devoted to the five modes of conduct, one should perform Vedic rites as the sole means for achieving the fruit of knowledge.
O dear one, he who places his cherished *liṅga* upon the palm of his hand and whose mental activity is absorbed therein, being indifferent to external activities, is a true *Vīraśaiva*. || 2 ||
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths.
Humans are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born are the most excellent. (1)
Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on sacrifice are superior.
Among those whose intellect is fixed on ritual sacrifices, the performers are [superior], but the renunciant is superior even to them. || 2 ||
Among them, the wise are the best; among them, the worshippers of Śaṅkara are the best.
Among them, the most excellent and highly fortunate are those who are united with my own form and limbs.
Among those who have attained union between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, one who possesses knowledge of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthalajñānavān*) shall be superior.
Therefore, there is nothing superior to this at any time throughout the three worlds. || 4 ||
Worthy of praise at all times and always to be honored by those who seek to conquer cyclic existence.
"What is the use of much speaking, my child? I am Śarva; of this there is no doubt. — Thus in the Pārameśvara.
He whose forehead possesses splendor, and on whose neck is a mark consisting of the letter 'ma'.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that by wearing Rudrākṣas on the body, one becomes "I am He" (Soham).
Thus, by the force of such authoritative means of knowledge, it is indeed established that the Vīraśaivas are the most excellent of all.
One who has strayed from the sacred revelation, having fallen into fear regarding the expiation prescribed by the revelation.
In order to gradually achieve the accomplishment of hearing [the teachings], a human being should bring forth the *manuṣya-tantra*.
For those men who have strayed from the path of the Vedas and are devoted to the path of the Tantras.
Therefore, that [Vedic path] is never for the left-hand way; indeed, for men who have utterly strayed from the Vedic path, the Pāñcarātra and other paths are provided by time itself.
The Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Yāmala, or the Ārhata—none of these are worthy of me.
And there are other such [teachings] as these, intended for the purpose of delusion. || 1 ||
And whatever adversaries there may be, they shall have their skulls made into ornaments.
Others are Śaivas and Pāśupatas, and likewise others are Pāñcarātras.
Likewise, all other evil-minded beings have their own presiding deities; furthermore, the duty of binding with nooses is ordained for the protection of the world.
Because they shatter that [truth], for that reason they are called heretics (pāṣaṇḍas).
Thus,
by such statements from the *Kūrma*, *Brahmakaivarta*, *Sūtasamhitā*, *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Laiṅga*, and *Pārāśara* Upapurāṇas.

Since resorting solely to the path of Tantra is irreproachable, and because the duties to be performed by Vīraśaivas are prescribed in such Tantras but are not seen among the Vedic Śruti and Smṛti scriptures,
[this applies] to those who are single-mindedly devoted to the performance of such duties.
If it is argued that the excellence of the Vīraśaivas is being propitiated [by this], it is not so;
for [the scriptures state]: "Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata..."

From the Mahābhārata statement, "Those who are equal in measure to oneself must not be slain by means of arguments," it follows that since the Pāñcarātra and other Āgamas— though censured by other Purāṇas— are established as authoritative,
the performance of the duties (dharma) proclaimed therein is necessarily established as mandatory. Not [otherwise].

And although, by virtue of the statement in the *Bhārata*, the conclusion is reached that only the *Pāñcarātra* and *Pāśupata* dharmas are to be practiced, the Vīraśaiva dharmas are not included within the *Pāñcarātra* or *Pāśupata* systems; therefore, for those who are solely intent upon the performance of dharma, [the Vīraśaiva path remains distinct].

Or rather, it should be stated that "superiority" [is established] because the statements prohibiting dualistic knowledge— distinguished as Vedic and non-Vedic— within the Pāśupata system are intended for the non-Vedic Pāśupatas,
whereas the injunctions are intended for the Vedic Pāśupatas and Vīraśaivas; this very distinction has been determined by the venerable Āpadeva in his commentary on the *Kalpataru*.
In the *Parimala* commentary on the *Adhikaraṇa* beginning with "patyu-rasāmañjasyāt" (Brahmasūtra 2.2.37), having explained the differences among the Pāśupata schools,
he then asserted therein that the *Laguḍīśa-pāśupata* system is to be accepted.
Therefore, being Tantric does not constitute the delimiting factor for the exclusion of the Vīraśaiva doctrines; indeed,
even the Laugākṣi Pāśupatas were accepted as being in accordance with the Vedas by the authors of the *Parimala* because they had received initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Furthermore, since even the Āgamas that propound the Vīraśaiva dharma are distinct from the Pāśupata [Āgamas] due to their posteriority, it follows that they are not to be accepted as being Vedic. Thus [the opponent] argues.
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi:
"Because they establish a single purpose through their unity, the authority of the Vedas and the Siddhāntas should always be understood as equal by the wise. — *Kriyāsāra*.
Or rather, from your ears, the auspicious Śiva-āgamas emerged like the breath of a cow.
They emerged directly from the mouths of Śiva himself.
The Nigamas and Āgamas spoken by Śiva have mutually non-contradictory meanings; yet, those of small intellect imagine a contradiction between them.
The authority of the Nigamas and Āgamas should be understood without distinction by the seers of reality, on account of their being the supreme instruction of the Self. || 4 ||

Since the authority of the Āgamas has been established— through descriptions consistent with the Vedas according to the words of the Ṛṣis, and by their being free from error in their exposition of Dharma, as well as by their having the Supreme Lord, the Soul of All, as their sole author— it follows that all the practices prescribed in the Āgamas must be accepted.
Thus, the status of being practiced according to the Vedic tradition is established. Otherwise, [there would be no authority] regarding the construction of temples for deities such as Śiva,

the installation of Śivaliṅgas and other icons, festivals and other rites, the extraction of mantras, the correction of mantra defects, the consecration of mantras, the application of mantras (nyāsa), and the procedures for ritual gestures (mudrā)— all of which are based solely on the Śiva Āgamas.
The activity of those who follow the Vedas would not be possible. Furthermore, in the *Śivamahātmyakhaṇḍa* of the *Sūtasamhitā*, following the conclusion of Vyāsa’s speech,
it is stated in the introduction that the son of Satyavatī is the author of the eighteen Purāṇas, just as he is the author of the various divisions beginning with the *Kāmika*.

"The god Maheśvara. In its commentary, Vidyāraṇya, for the purpose of generating confidence in the words of Vyāsa, begins with the eighteen [Tantras] and establishes the authority of the Śaiva Āgamas, such as the Kāmika and others, on the grounds that they were spoken by Śiva, as follows:

Thus, it has been established that the eighteen Purāṇas composed by Vyāsa, who is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, possess authority. Therefore, the necessity of practicing the Vīraśaiva duties as taught in the Āgamas is proven. And so, in those Āgamas:
Among the seven types of Śaivas— namely, the Ādiśaiva, Anādiśaiva, Māhāśaiva, Anuśaiva, Avāntaraśaiva, Pravaraśaiva, and Antyaśaiva—
who are distinguished by differences in their conduct, there are the Sāmānyaśaiva, Miśraśaiva, and Śuddhaśaiva.
Among the four types [of Śaivas] categorized by way of their Vīraśaiva form—

specifically, among the three types of Vīraśaivas distinguished as Sāmānya-Vīraśaiva, Viśeṣa-Vīraśaiva, and Nirābhāsa-Vīraśaiva— the practice to be performed thereafter consists of the wearing of sacred ash (bhasma) and rudrākṣa beads, and the [recitation of the] five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī).

The common Vīraśaiva duties— consisting of the recitation of mantras (*japa*), the wearing of the *liṅga*, the worship of the *guru-liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*, and the acceptance of the sanctified water from their feet (*pādodaka*) as nectar— are established in the *Kālāgnirudropaniṣad*,
the *Bhasmajābālopaniṣad*, the *Cidambaropaniṣad*, the *Vedāntasāra*, and other Upaniṣads which expound the wearing of the *liṅga* and related practices.

Furthermore, it is extensively established in the Taittirīya and other mantras, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, Sūtasaṃhitā, Śivarahasya, Liṅgapurāṇa, and others; in the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula; and in the Virashaiva traditions designated as the "Worshipful Name" (Nāmārādhya).
Thus, its Vedic character is established.

Otherwise, those Brāhmaṇas who are considered Vedic but who perform Tantric rites such as *stotra*, *chāva*, and *pratiṣṭhā* would not possess Vedic character. And so it is; the same logic applies to that.
She said: "Is it not the case that even in the performance of Tantric dharma, there is an irreducible Vedic character?

For the Śrutis and Āgamas that propound the Virasaiva dharma possess designations such as 'general,' 'particular,' 'without support,' and 'equal,' due to differences in their modes of conduct. [The devotee...]
Of the Maheśvara-prāsāda, Prāṇaliṅgin, Śaraṇaikya-sthalas, and of the Liṅga-sthalas designated as Ācāra-liṅga, Guru-liṅga, Śiva-liṅga, Jaṅgama-liṅga, Prasāda-liṅga, and Mahā-liṅga,
as well as of the previously mentioned Aṅga-sthalas, there is the practice of progressively higher dharmas.

For the ancients (*pūrva-ṛṣi*), following the practice of the ancient dharma, there was a gradual development; thus, the practice of such dharma consisted in the performance of a synthesis of Vedic and Tantric duties, such as the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the wearing of the *liṅga*, as practiced in regions like Kālahasti and Śrīśaila.

If it is asked: "Since it cannot be worshipped by anyone other than the Supreme (Parameśvara), how can it have as its sole object the Vīraśaivas who are not [directly] the Worshippable One?"—[the answer is: "He proclaimed to those beyond the stages of life (atyāśramins) that which is supremely pure and well-received by the assembly of sages," according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad; for the atyāśramin is [one who is so] at all times.
Regarding the term *atyāśramī* heard in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad—"One should recite [the mantra] once"—it refers to those beyond the stages of life (*āśrama*), namely:

the student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣuka*); and among these, the wise one who transcends both caste and stage of life (*ātivarṇāśramī*) is the most excellent. (1)
Even for you who dwell in the forest, O Lotus-born One, there is no moment [of peace] while remaining a householder.
One becomes a guru only through the power of the excellence of knowledge, and not otherwise.
O Hari, the same applies to those in the forest-dweller stage of life (vānaprastha) as well as to renunciants (saṃnyāsins).
One becomes a guru solely through the power of the excellence of one's knowledge, and not otherwise.
The Guru is declared to be beyond the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī) for all who possess the qualification [for initiation].
Even he would not be the best, O Puruṣottama, as I am.
He who transcends the castes and stages of life is called the Guru of the true gurus.
He for whom the conduct of the castes and stages of life has dissolved through the vision of his own Self.
Abiding within his own self, he [perceives] all the various stages of life (āśramas) belonging to those of his own caste.
The man who, having transcended his own stages of life and social classes, is established in the Self; || 6 ||
The four castes and stages of life have been proclaimed by those who expound the meaning of all the Vedas.
The five-syllabled supreme knowledge (parāvidyā) is for the attainment of the light of Śiva.
The syllable *voṃ* is the subtle *praṇava*, the supreme seed of all sciences.
Therefore, one should purify all principles without exception by means of the *praṇava*.
He sprinkles his body with water while reciting the seven verses beginning with "Agni" (agnir ityādi).
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the mantra: "The triple life-span of Jamadagni."
One should meditate within oneself upon Śambhu, the Lord, the Auspicious One, the Supreme Peace, who has Umā as his companion.
They call this body, whose limbs are smeared with ashes and which transcends the conduct of the [four] stages of life, "Viṣṇu. Thus they speak.
This is the highest stage of life among all four stages; by this vow, one abandons both the state of being a beast and the actual beast itself.
Then, having purified all the principles (tattvas) once more with the syllable Om (praṇava), ||
And he should establish himself within the stainless Supreme Lord.

Having washed their own bodies with the water of knowledge, they [attain liberation]; this is the Pāśupata yoga for the sake of release from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu). "This is the essence of all Vedāntas; it is beyond all exertion," so says the Śruti.
"Knowledge arises for him by whom the Pāśupata vow has been properly practiced with joy;

through that, there is liberation from bonds"— such statements from the Kāmika, Skānda, and Liṅga Purāṇas, as well as the Śiva Āgamas, [establish] that [this applies] even to those beyond the stages of life (ativarṇāśramin).
Because it establishes superiority over those whose nature is the practice of the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma).

The state of being a "supreme ascetic" (*ātyāśramitva*), which originates from the fifth face [of Śiva], culminates in the Vīraśaivas who possess the fifth stage of life (*pañcamāśrama*); therefore, there is no room for doubt regarding the supremacy of the aforementioned object of worship. For this very reason, the previously cited passage beginning with "from worms, insects, and moths," and so forth, establishes the excellence of the Vīraśaivas.

The statements in the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā conclude with unerring certainty. Now, one might object: "Do not the scriptural, traditional, and Puranic texts that establish the various stages of life (āśramas) also conclude with those very same [conclusions]? However—"

In the case of Brahmins who observe the conduct of their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) and are worthy of worship, [the fruits of action] culminate in that; even when they are empty [of such qualities], they likewise culminate there.
For instance, in the phrase "the conduct of caste and stage of life," [it refers to] Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.

The Śūdras constitute the four castes. For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is the entitlement to the study of the Vedas, the performance of meditations, and fruitful ritual acts, according to the distinctions of the stages of life (āśrama): studenthood (brahmacarya), householdership (gārhasthya), forest-dwelling (vānaprastha), and renunciation (saṃnyāsa). These are the four stages of life.
Dwelling in the house of a teacher of reality, practicing mendicancy, and the study of the Vedas and so forth constitute the duties of the first stage of life (brahmacarya).

The rites to be performed include the *garbhadāna* and others; the seven *pākayajñas*, the seven *haviryajñas*, and the seven *saṃsthās*; and within the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajñas*), the eight forms and the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*).

Furthermore, the six duties consisting of sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts constitute the dharma of the second stage of life (āśrama).

The dharma of the third stage of life (*tṛtīyāśrama*) consists of dwelling in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, wearing matted hair and deerskin, performing such penances as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, and—

preceded by the renunciation of the duties of the three previously mentioned stages— the inquiry into Brahman, the practice of begging for alms, and the avoidance of passion, hatred, and other such afflictions.
Devotion to sacred literature, dwelling alone for one night, and the practice of yoga and so forth constitute the duties of the fourth stage of life (caturthāśrama).

Regarding the phrase *ātivarṇāśramācārāḥ*, the term *ati* here signifies "transcending" (*atikrānta*) the conduct (*ācāra*) of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). According to the rules of Pāṇinian grammar, the second member of a compound takes the form *ati* in the sense of "transcending. This [term] should be applied to the meaning of the word in accordance with the established linguistic conventions. It applies specifically to those who, while still existing among those who practice the aforementioned duties (*dharma*), have transcended them.

How can the application of words such as "caste" (*varṇa*), "stage of life" (*āśrama*), and "conduct" (*ācāra*)— which depend upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*)— be justified in the case of Vīraśaivas who, through their connection with Yoga, have transcended that which is to be propitiated? For words that denote specific entities necessarily require a counter-correlative relation.

If it is argued that such esteem exists only among the Śālis because of their fitness for conduct, [we reply: those who have transcended the conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) exist above and beyond; they are indeed direct Mahādevas who rejoice in the Agamas. Since they were born from the fifth mouth of the Five-faced One, these Pañcamas are superior to all the castes.
My devotees are always dear to me; Śiva is the Liṅga, the sacred field is the body, and their union is the substratum.

Therefore, the beauty of the union between the *liṅga* and the body is the sole devotion to the path of liberation. Because of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between the *liṇga* and the body, the wearing of the *liṅga* upon the body is [the mark of a true ascetic].
Consequently, even one who is joined with the *liṅga* and the body through this very discipline becomes a possessor of all stages of life (*sarvāśramī*). || 1 ||
From the perspective of Īśāna, there is the splendor of the limbs of the Liṅgas born of the lineage of Gaṇas, which are solely intent upon the path to liberation.

By wearing the *liṅga* upon the body through the constant practice of the union (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and the limbs, and by performing this as a religious observance (*niyama*), they were liberated from the bonds of *saṃsāra*. || 2 ||

Thus, since it is possible to correctly state that the terms *vīra*, *śaiva*, *āmnāya*, *atiśrama*, *ācāra*, and so forth, are synonymous with the Vedic terms cited in the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, as well as in the *Kriyāsāra*, the *Udāhṛta-vedāntasāra*, the *Upaniṣads*, and other such texts, [the identity of these traditions is established].
Furthermore, the term "one who has transcended the stages of life" (atyāśramin) does not apply to those who are merely performing the duties belonging to a specific stage of life.
As for what was stated—that [the word "Brahman"] possesses a counter-correlate (sapratyogī)—that is untenable;

for since there can be no absence of impurities (apāpmatva) that would serve as a counter-correlate to Brahman in the case of words such as "water" (āpaḥ) and so forth, those words could not function [to denote it]. And if that were the case, then [there would be no basis for] the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma).

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the grammatical rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), because [in this case] the status of being denotable by words such as *atyāśrama* is consistent even in the absence of an actual counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the human stages of life (*āśrama*), since— as in the cases of Śuka and Vāmadeva— it is postulated that they performed the duties of their respective castes and stages of life in previous births.
This would contradict the grammatical injunctions. Furthermore, it should not be argued that, by thus establishing the consistency of the meaning of the term *atyāśramin*,
those other than Vīraśaivas— namely, other renunciants (*virakta*), the wise (*jñānin*), and even Śūdras—
would also attain the status of *atyāśramin*.

Because the word *atyāśramin*— which possesses a meaning obstructed by the understanding derived from the three [scriptural] statements that it transcends the conduct of the castes and stages of life—
is improper to apply through its mere etymological derivation (*yoga*), just as the word *paṅkaja* [is not applied] to grass or a blue lotus.

This is according to the maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga). For this very reason, by the rule of the sūtra *na śabdasya anhaḥ khaḥ kratv-ādau*, the term *ahīna*—which denotes a collection of days (*ahargaṇa*) such as the *dvirātra* and *trirātra* sacrifices—is not applied through etymology (*yoga*) to refer to a sacrifice consisting of a single day or similar durations. Thus, it refers exclusively to sacrifices accomplished over multiple days.

The principle that "agency belongs to another" and that "the *ahīna* sacrifice [is primary] because of the context"— this very logic was established in the section beginning with "the secondary [meaning] is [used] because of the context" (*guṇaḥ syāt prakaraṇāt*) in the third chapter of the *Pūrvatantra*.

Therefore, the term *atyāśramin* (one who has transcended the stages of life) is applicable to the Vīraśaivas; for even by the power of yoga, their status as supreme Vīraśaivas can be established. Indeed, it is stated thus in the *Pādmapurāṇa* regarding worship: [text follows].

By the *Amara-kośa* [which states] "the root *su* is used in the sense of worship" (*svati pūjāyām*), and by the grammatical derivation [of the term *āśrama*] as "those whose conduct (*ācāra*) belongs to the stages of life (*varṇa-āśrama*) that have been highly honored (*ātiśayita*)," these scriptural statements do not refer to the Pāśupata [practice], which is to be performed according to the procedure prescribed in the *Atharvaśiras*.

The other synonym is the state of having completely renounced the entire cycle of worldly existence preceded by the knowledge of one's own Self; this applies to one who is devoid of the wearing of ashes, the assumption of any particular caste-mark (*liṅga*), or the like— whether such marks are present or absent—
in relation to the venerable Brahmin.

Alternatively, since [the terms] can denote either the exclusive state of being a *atyāśramin* (one who has transcended the stages of life) or the connection with it, they must be understood as propounding the *Kevala-Vīraśaiva* tradition; for those Brahmins who possess the duties of their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) are worthy of being designated by the term *atyāśramin*. O Supreme Lord, fifth-faced one!

O Saṃbhūta, Pramatha-gaṇanāyaka, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Gajakarṇa, Reṇuka, Dāruka! For those born into the Gotras [of these], who exclusively practice the duties of their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama-dharma) as prescribed for Vīraśaivas alone, it is appropriate that the Śruti, Āgamas, and Purāṇas designate them by the term "atyāśramin" (one who has transcended the stages of life).
Furthermore, the hosts of Pramathas, who have emerged from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, are by no means like ordinary human beings.
Since there is an absence of the acceptance of wives according to the *prākṛta* (natural/ordinary) rule, how can these [beings] be born of that lineage?
Even so, if they do exist, then it must be stated that even the *ārādhya* Brahmins are born of that lineage:
"To Dvārāpā, who touches Dvārāpā, svāhā! To Dvārāpī, who touches Dvārāpī, svāhā!"
In the rite known as Khāhitīśanabala, the object denoted by the word *dvārāpa* exists because Nandikeśvara and his wife— Suyasā, who is well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts—
are present there, just as the Supreme Lord assumes forms such as that of a Kirāta for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world.

Because it is possible for even those who are purely Vīraśaivas to be born into that lineage through the acquisition of an ordinary wife; however, since being born into that lineage is in every way improper for Brahmins who are to be worshipped, if [that were the case]...

If it is argued that one possesses the status of being born into that lineage because of the pride of practicing the Vīraśaiva dharma, then there would be no such status of being born into those lineages as established by the creation of *gotras*— such as Vaiśvāmitra, Bhārgava, Bhāradvāja, Āgastya, Āṅgirasa, and Vāsiṣṭha. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, for one does not seek refuge in the shade of a tree out of fear of a scorpion.
There might be a downfall like a fall into the mouth of a venomous serpent for pride, and there would likewise be a destruction of one's Brahminhood.

Nor should it be said that both descent from a lineage of sages (*ṛṣi*) and descent from a lineage of attendants (*pramatha*) are possible for us, who are worshipped by Brahmins; why then is it even mentioned, let alone claimed, that we are descended from both lineages?
Or by means of the tradition of the disciples.

Not the first [alternative], because it is established by the Śruti text, "He is born from a donkey; therefore the donkey has double seed," that both types of potency would arise individually like a donkey; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of being laughed at as a mere low-caste person (antyajātīya). Nor the second, because such a tradition could be understood figuratively, and thus even a member of the fourth caste (śūdra) might be possible [under that interpretation].
Therefore, because the exclusive Vīraśaivas are born of the lineage of the Gaṇas.

Listen, O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, to these leaders of my Gaṇas from the latter portion of the Kāmika Āgama. Having been appointed by me to go to the world of mortals among all the various castes, some of these Gaṇas were born; others, having manifested within Liṅgas and images, became devoted to worship and meditation upon the Liṅga, and established it.
The path of Vīraśaiva,
which bestows liberation upon the earth.
"For the benefit and welfare of all living beings, they bear the five mudrās;
they possess the knowledge of the six locations, and their forms are mobile from the beginningless past."
In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā: "O child, these leaders of the Gaṇas, having gone to the surface of the earth, have been appointed by me;
they have been born into all castes, yet they remain devoted once again to the worship of the Liṅga."
Having established [this work], O Supreme Hero-Śaiva, I behold your state for the benefit of men.
Carrying the five mudrās, they wander about, thinking, "I shall reach him."

Therefore, it is entirely logical that he is designated by the term "atyāśramī" (one who has transcended the stages of life) and possesses all the aforementioned qualities. For this very reason, it is most appropriate to cite here those very scriptural authorities and logical arguments favorable to what was stated previously. To illustrate: [they are] "pure" and "natural," and so forth.

Human beings are traditionally held to be of two kinds: those purified by the rites of Śiva are considered pure, while others are regarded as belonging to the realm of Prakṛti; for the state of those possessing the duties of caste, stage of life, and so forth, is indeed considered twofold.
This was formerly taught by Ekāśiva and declared by Brahmā as the steadfastness in the dharma spoken by Śiva for those established in the Śiva-āśrama.
For the Śiva-saṃskāra is remembered as having various dharmas that encompass all things. Thus it is said.

Therefore, due to their distinction based on the difference between natural and supernatural attributes, the Vīraśaivas born of the Gaṇa lineage— who are not subject to the natural [social order], who are denoted by the term *varṇāśrama*,
and who belong to the fifth stage of life (*pañcamāśramin*)— possess that which is uncommon to others.
Since its status as supreme among all things is indeed established, there is no room for doubt or anger.

Therefore, that doctrine of his is the most excellent in every way; likewise, there is no other system equal to Vīraśaivism in the three worlds—a meritorious path that bestows all enjoyments and grants union with Śiva. || 1 ||
Just as there is no man equal to me among men, nor any woman equal to you among women, so too, O Vīraśaiva, it is my conviction that there is nothing equal to you.
Even after committing hundreds of sins, whether intentionally or unintentionally, one who has attained the Vīraśaiva doctrine is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
Because by the mere wearing of the *liṅga*, one attains the state of Śiva.
O Goddess, my doctrine is Śaiva, which bestows immediate liberation.
Just as the auspicious Bhāgīrathī is the most meritorious among all rivers, O Śivā.
Just as I am toward all women among men. || 5 ||
Just as Manikarṇikā is the foremost among sacred sites in Kāśī, so is my five-syllabled mantra the foremost among all mantras; and just as our abode on Kailāsa is supreme among all worlds.
O Goddess, the Vīraśaiva doctrine is the most supreme of all for me. || 7 ||

Thus, by the words of the *Pārameśvara-virāgama* and by the statements of the Śruti, Āgamas, and Purāṇas augmented by the previously mentioned logic, it is established that the Virāśaiva doctrine possesses supreme excellence, just as Śiva’s status as the highest among all deities is established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and logic.

One who is devoted solely to that [path] follows the Vīraśaiva conduct, which is threefold according to the divisions of Sāmānya-Vīraśaiva, Viśeṣa-Vīraśaiva, and Nirābhāra-Vīraśaiva. O Goddess, by following this very path, one should daily perform the wearing of sacred ashes, the wearing of rudrākṣa beads, and the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra; this is the established doctrine.

"One should wear the *liṅga* of the gurus with great care. O Pārvatī, a Vīraśaiva should perform worship by unifying the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *prāṇaliṅga*, and the *bhāvaliṅga*; there is no distinction [between them]. Since the general characteristics of a Vīraśaiva are established by such statements, [the definition follows].
Whether it be oneself, one’s children, ornaments, or wealth— whatever one’s own cherished possession may be—
one should offer that to the mobile [deities].

"Having subsequently taken what was experienced by them, one should personally perform for oneself that which is known as *prasāda*, characterized by a specific understanding. Because of such statements, the definition of Viśeṣa-Vīraśaiva is established. [They may be] those with matted hair (*jaṭin*), those with shaven heads (*muṇḍin*), or those with tufts of hair (*śikhin*), clad in saffron robes (*kāṣāyavasana*), free from pride (*niṣpraha*).
One who possesses only his own [inner] organ, subsists on alms, is free from fear, remains silent, is endowed with compassion, and is without worldly burdens— he is known as a *nirābhāra*.
Wearing a patched garment and carrying a water-pot, he was endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.

"One who carries a staff and a loincloth is known as a *nirābhāra*. Thus, through such statements from the *Sūkṣmataṃtra* and other scriptures, the characteristics of the *vīraśaiva* *nirābhāra* are established.
In relation to the Sāmānya, Viśeṣa, and Vīra Śaivas, [the devotee] is denoted by such terms as *cara* (mobile) and *jaṅgama* (animate).
The Nirābhāra-Vīraśaiva is the supreme teacher; that he is the most excellent among all due to his dispassion is beyond dispute. Furthermore, [it is stated] in the Śivarahasya:
The form of the Liṅga that has been prescribed, however, is the Jaṅgama-prāṇa-liṅga.
The Guru is said to be the liṅga of being; though it is of three kinds, it is declared to be one.
When the cause has arrived.
O Lord of Teachers, one should recognize the embodied forms [of the Divine] as Saccidānanda.
One should contemplate that ever-perfect grace within the state of one's own self. || 1 ||
In the *Vīrāgama*.
The *liṅga* of the body and the *liṅga* of the Guru are said to be threefold, yet they are one.
In the *Siddhāntasikhāmaṇi*.
Śiva alone is the manifest Lord who bestows grace upon all.
The Guru, whose self is the mobile Liṅga, exists as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

By such statements as these, the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama— who are of the nature of *saccidānanda*— are accepted as non-different from the Supreme Lord’s own nature, just as Brahman, though characterized by the attributes of *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda*, is not differentiated from them in its essential being, despite appearing distinct due to the defects of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
In the same way, although the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama appear distinct, according to the injunctions of the scriptures and in reality,

their essential oneness is established. Furthermore, with respect to the nature of one's own self— which is of the nature of existence (sat) characterized by non-sublation throughout the three periods of time— it is of the nature of consciousness (cit) by virtue of being self-luminous.

Because the Lord, who is the seer of the heart, is self-luminous, and because he possesses the state of being desired by all seekers and the state of being the giver of supreme valid knowledge, he exists solely as the very nature of bliss in both those forms;
thus, just as he alone is most venerable, so too is the Reality (Tattva) that conforms to him.
The state of being most venerable among all; for it is said thus in the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi:
The Liṅga is said to be of two kinds, by way of being mobile (jaṅgama) and immobile (ajaṅgama).
That which is the immobile Liṅga is fashioned from stone and other such materials. || 1 ||
Therefore, that mobile linga known as the Śivayogin is superior; indeed, I shall now declare the excellence of both the [stationary] linga and the mobile one. || 2 ||
The mobile form of knowledge, however, is the *liṅga*; thus it is stated in the *Svāyambhūvāgama*.
Two types of signs have been described: the moving and the non-moving.
Due to its superior form, the moving is [superior], while the non-moving consists of the earth and so forth. (1)
Maheśvara always dwells there indeed, filled with affection.
In the practice of mantra-refinement, Sadāśiva himself remains present.
Also from the Śivadharmaśāstra:
Maheśvara always dwells there, ever endowed with affection.
In practice, Maheśvara is to be known constantly through the purificatory rites of mantra.
In the *Śivarahasya*: "The term *pada* is known to mean both the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is the essence of all things."
Just as there is an interval between those two, so it is with this moving linga.
The linga is said to be of two kinds: the stationary and the mobile.
Through the contempt shown toward the mobile, the immobile becomes fruitless.
In the Śaivaratnākara.
The Liṅga-field is the abode of the Guru, and the Guru-field is the mobile [Liṅga].
Though carrying the burden of moving through the world, he is free from the weight of burdens.
Thus [ends] the *Śivadharmaśāstra*, the crest-jewel of the Siddhāntas, within the *Svāyaṃbhūvāgama*.

And by the statements in the *Śivarahasya* and other texts, the greatness of the stationary linga (*svarūpaliṅga*), which is of two kinds and is the locus for the consecration of mantras, is [greater] than that of the mobile linga (*caraliṅga*)— the mobile linga being one that is endowed with the knowledge of the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*) at all times.

The preeminence of that which is denoted by the term "the moving" (jaṅgama) is indeed established; for this very reason, there are such scriptural statements as: "In the Rigveda, in the seed, in the linga, in the body of the Guru, in the yogi of Śiva, and in the physical body, Śiva is ever present," and "Whatever the knower of Brahman eats, he consumes the entire universe unto its furthest limits."
In the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*), there are many passages that establish the superiority of one endowed with knowledge (*jñānin*).
In the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, this lunar day of Śiva is most venerable; for indeed, there is no greater delight for the feet in the three worlds than on this day. (Vīrāgama)
One should prepare the *prasāda* of the mobile [deity] for the purpose of the food offering (*naivedya*);
indeed, I shall now describe the specific procedure for bathing the lotus feet with water.
In the Pārameśvara [Tantra].
The playful washing of the feet and the supreme immersion of the liṅga.
The prasāda and the food offering (naivedya) from that [deity] likewise certainly yield the fruit of liberation. || 1 ||
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
For mobile beings, the holy water of the feet is the supreme bathing of the *liṅga*.
O Great Goddess, that which is offered as a food-oblation (naivedya) by His grace is remembered as bestowing auspiciousness. || 1 ||
Therefore, by the grace of the mobile liṅga, there shall be my offering.
Consecration, water, and bathing—this specific distinction of mine is now being told. || 2 ||
Thus, by such statements from the medical scriptures (*vaidyaśāstra*), the *Virāgama*, the *Pārameśvara*, the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*, and other texts,
the bathing with the water from the feet of the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*,
as well as the offering of that grace (*prasāda*), are established in preference to the *liṅga* itself.

Indeed, the superiority of the mobile [liṅga] is already established, because these statements are heard in the context of the worship of the chosen liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga). Therefore, by virtue of the context, the washing with the water from the feet of the mobile [liṅga],
as well as the offering of grace (prasāda), apply specifically to the chosen liṅga, and not to the fixed liṅga, because the latter is non-natural (aprākṛta).

If it is argued that a mortal who worships a fixed *liṅga* is not pure for the rites of a formal assembly (*paṅkti-karma*), [we reply: a mortal who worships a mobile *liṅga* is a purifier in the rites of a formal assembly. Having touched a funeral pyre, wood from a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), or even a temple-priest (*devalaka*), one should enter the water with one's clothes on.

"He who performs the worship of a deity as a profession shall indeed be called a *devalaka*, excluded from all ritual acts. Because one who worships a fixed, consecrated *liṅga* is designated by the term *devalaka* according to such passages, [there must be] avoidance of cohabitation and communal dining with him.

Because it establishes that [the wearer] is excluded from all ritual acts such as touchability; because prohibitions are observed regarding dwelling together with a Vīramāheśvara who has assumed the *liṅga*, as well as eating in the same row and so forth;
and because it establishes his superiority over others through purity and other qualities—[this refers to] the worship of the chosen *liṅga* (iṣṭaliṅga) and the fixed *liṅga* (sthiraliṅga).

In order to demonstrate the superiority of the agents, the superiority and inferiority of the desired stable *liṅga* and [the mobile] must respectively be determined; and thus, [the superiority] of the mobile reality over all [others]...
